feedback: If the learner says the vapour 'disappears', show that in the follow-one-droplet view the tagged droplet is still there, just rendered faint — hidden as a clear gas, not gone.
If the learner says clouds ARE the vapour, point out the vapour is faint/near-invisible while the cloud is made of visible tiny water droplets (or ice crystals) that formed when the vapour cooled.
If the learner expects rain to be the end, run the droplet round again so they see it flow back and re-evaporate: the loop has no end.
If the learner thinks the water moves by itself, have them turn the Sun control down and notice the whole engine slow — the Sun is the driver.
activities.intendedInsight: The water cycle is an endless loop driven by the Sun's energy, and the same water is conserved — it only changes form (liquid↔invisible vapour) and place, never being used up or destroyed.
learnerActions: Over a land-and-sea scene, raise a Sun/heat control and watch puddles and sea surfaces give off vapour that rises, cools into clouds, and falls as rain that flows back to the sea.
Turn the Sun control down and observe the whole loop slow: evaporation slows, fewer clouds form, and rain becomes less — stating in your own words why.

Switch to a 'follow one droplet' view: tag a single glowing droplet and watch it evaporate, become near-invisible vapour, condense inside a cloud, fall as rain, and flow back to the start again — never disappearing.

Watch a drying puddle on a hard surface and describe out loud where the water goes (UP into the air as invisible vapour), rather than saying it just vanished. (On soil, some puddle water also soaks into the ground.)
activities.title: Sun-driven water-cycle model the learner controls

feedback: If the learner predicts the water is destroyed or 'used up', revisit with a covered dish: droplets usually appear on the underside of the lid when it is cooler than the water — hidden, not gone.
If the learner thinks the can's droplets came from inside, point to their clear colour versus the coloured water inside: coloured water cannot pass through and arrive clear.

When interpreting the result, note that droplets form readily on the cold surface in typical humid indoor air but fewer may appear in very dry air, so judge by what you actually observe rather than expecting a guaranteed outcome.
Reinforce that clouds and the white 'steam' (mist) you can see above a kettle are tiny condensed water droplets (clouds may also hold ice crystals); the vapour itself is a clear gas you cannot see.
activities.intendedInsight: Evaporated water becomes invisible vapour in the air (it doesn't vanish), and 'sweating' on a cold surface is water condensing FROM the surrounding air, not water seeping through the container.
learnerActions: Before observing a puddle (or a shallow dish of water) left in a warm, sunny spot, predict and write down what will happen to the water and WHY.

Watch over time as it dries, then explain where the water went — into the air as invisible vapour. (Water in a dish cannot soak away, so it can only have gone into the air; a puddle on soil or grass can also lose some water by soaking into the ground.)
Add a few drops of food colouring to ice water in a can or cup, then watch for droplets forming on the OUTSIDE of the cold surface and check their colour.
Explain why any outside droplets are CLEAR, not coloured: the water condensed from the air onto the cold surface — it did not leak through the wall.
activities.title: Drying puddle and cold-can discrepant-event investigation

feedback: If the learner changes more than one thing (amount of water, dish size, surface area, air flow or location), remind them a fair test keeps everything the same except the one variable being tested — here, temperature.
If the learner compares a sunny with a shaded dish and calls it a temperature test, point out that sunlight differs too; to test temperature alone, warm the water while matching the lighting.
Connect the result back to the whole cycle: more heat speeds evaporation, just as the Sun's warmth does on a hot day.
activities.intendedInsight: Under matched conditions, warmer water evaporates faster, so the rate of evaporation rises with temperature. In everyday life a hot day speeds drying, and on a sunny day both the warmth and the direct sunlight raise the rate — the Sun's heat is what warms water and drives the cycle.
learnerActions: Fill two similar open dishes with the same amount of water — one with warm water and one with cool water — keeping dish size, surface area, air flow and location the same so that only the water temperature differs.
Predict which will lose water faster and why.

Check them over time (e.g. mark or measure the water level) and compare which lost water faster, remembering that the warm water slowly cools towards room temperature, so the difference may be small and is clearest early on.
State your conclusion from what you observed: if the warmer dish lost more water, this supports the idea that higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation.

As a separate question about the Sun's role, compare a puddle in the sun with one in the shade (observing the puddles on the ground) and discuss which dries faster and why — remembering the puddles may also differ in size and depth.
activities.title: Fair test: does temperature change how fast water evaporates?

feedback: If the diagram only shows an ocean arrow, prompt: where else does water evaporate from? (wet land, puddles, plants).
If the diagram is a one-way line ending at rain, ask how the fallen rain gets back up — close the loop.
If the Sun is missing, ask what provides the energy to lift the water as vapour.
Talking a droplet through 'where do you go next, and are you ever destroyed?' can surface conservation; keep it anchored to the real causes (heat drives it, cooling condenses it).
activities.intendedInsight: The water cycle is one continuous, conserved system — water evaporates from many sources (sea, land, plants), condenses, precipitates and flows back, driven by the Sun, with none lost.
learnerActions: Draw your own diagram of the water cycle from memory, labelling arrows for where water goes.
Compare it with a closed-loop cross-section showing land, sea and sky, then add any missing arrows — especially evaporation from land and plants, not just the ocean.
Draw the loop so it has no beginning and no end, and mark the Sun as the engine that drives it.
Optionally extend by adding runoff, groundwater and transpiration from plants as parts of one conserved system.
Explain to a partner, or to an imagined water droplet, where the water goes next and whether it is ever destroyed.
activities.title: Draw, revise and trace your own water-cycle diagram
